What Not to Do With AI

Wil RandolphAugust 7, 2026
ShareLinkedInXFacebookEmail

An acquaintance recently told me that he uses AI agents to write his blog posts. He asked why I do not do the same, and the question was not hostile or even especially provocative; to him, it seemed practical. The tools exist, they are fast, and they can produce polished prose on almost any subject. If the goal is simply to keep publishing, why not let the machine help carry the load?

My answer was that I do use AI, but not that way.

I may use AI to clean up an audio recording after I have rambled through an idea while driving, walking, or trying to catch a thought before it disappears. I may use it to help shape a rough note into a grammatically coherent sentence, or to organize a scattered reflection into a structure that another person can follow. I may even use it to create a related image for a post. Those uses do not bother me because the raw material is still mine: the experience, the judgment, the concern, the lesson, the question. AI, in that context, is assisting the expression of thought rather than replacing the act of thinking.

That distinction matters. People do not read my writing because they are curious what an AI system might generate about a topic. They read it, if they read it at all, because they expect something that came through me: my knowledge, my mistakes, my experiences, my interpretations, and the conclusions I have reached after living with a problem long enough to have something useful to say about it. I do not write to fill space on the internet. I write because I am trying to impart knowledge, or at least share enough of what I have gone through that someone else might avoid one of my pitfalls or benefit from one of my successes.

If I gave that work to an AI agent and published the result under my name, I would not simply be using a tool. I would be allowing a tool to impersonate my contribution. That would be misleading to the reader, but it would also be corrosive to me, because it would train me to confuse output with insight and visibility with value. Over time, I would be devaluing the very thing I am supposed to bring to the page: not perfect prose, not constant content, but a mind shaped by experience and willing to be accountable for what it says.

This becomes even more troubling when people apply the same habit to business advice. My first advice to a business owner has never been to build agents and let AI start blogging before anyone understands the customers, the business objectives, or the market. The first questions are more basic and more important: What are you trying to build? Who are you trying to reach? What problem are you solving? What does the customer already believe, fear, want, misunderstand, or need? What would make a qualified prospect trust you enough to take the next step?

If AI helps answer those questions, organize research, test assumptions, summarize interviews, or clarify messaging, then use it. That is a legitimate use of the tool because it supports the work of understanding. But using AI to create the illusion that the business is active, successful, insightful, or strategically clear when none of that work has been done is a lie. It hurts the business owner because it encourages them to mistake activity for progress, and it hurts prospective clients and customers because it asks them to trust a performance rather than a real understanding of their needs.

There is also a simpler possibility that people do not like to admit: if you cannot write what you need to say, perhaps you should not say anything yet. That does not mean every person must be a gifted stylist or publish without help. It means that before you put your name on an idea, there should be an idea there that belongs to you. If your only reason for publishing is that you believe you must have a post this week, and your solution is to let AI auto-generate one so your calendar looks disciplined, then the issue is no longer technology. The issue is integrity.

Posting today instead of tomorrow will not change the outcome of your business meeting. It will not make you a better salesperson, and it certainly will not make you look smarter. If the post has no real insight, no real audience, and no real connection to the work you are trying to do, then all you have done is add more content to the digital trash heap. You may have filled a dead space on your social feed, but filling space is not the same as creating value.

This is especially important for business owners who mistake activity for traction. AI can help you produce content at ten times the rate, and at first that may feel like progress. You look busy. Your feed looks alive. Your impressions may even go up. But then what? Did engagement actually improve, or did a platform merely show your posts to more people for a while because you posted more often? Did you get more likes, and if so, did any of those likes convert into calls, meetings, referrals, DMs, qualified leads, or sales? Or did you get roughly the same response you always get, from roughly the same people, with a little more noise around the edges?

The uncomfortable question is whether you are measuring the outcome or simply admiring the motion. If your business is in Singapore and your impressions are coming from Palm Beach, Florida, did that help you, or did it only make a dashboard look encouraging for a few seconds? Do you even know where the attention is coming from, who is engaging, whether they can buy from you, or whether they are merely passing by? AI-generated content can create the appearance of reach while doing nothing to deepen trust, clarify your offer, or move the right person closer to a decision.

That is the trap. You are not necessarily becoming more engaged, more informed, more persuasive, or more relevant. You may simply be using AI to keep up the appearance of being those things. The feed looks active, but the business is not stronger. The content pipeline is full, but the thinking is empty. The metrics flicker, but no one meaningful is moved.

Does that make you feel smart, or does it make you feel like a poser? I ask that seriously, because the answer matters. If you feel uneasy, that discomfort is probably telling you something useful. If you feel nothing at all about presenting machine-generated thought as your own, then I question less your intelligence than your ethical framework. A byline should mean something. It should signal that a person stood behind the thinking, not merely that a person approved the upload.

The public conversation about AI needs more precision. The issue is not whether people should use AI; they already do, and in many cases they should. AI can help people communicate more clearly, overcome technical barriers, summarize complex material, translate between languages, and move through tedious work that once consumed hours. Used well, it can make people more capable. Used poorly, however, it can help people perform capability they have not actually developed.

That is the first thing not to do with AI: do not use it to fake a point of view. A point of view is not a content category or a prompt template. It is the product of attention, experience, conflict, failure, reflection, and judgment. When AI generates an essay in your voice about something you have not seriously considered, the result may sound impressive, but it is hollow in the one place that matters. It has the appearance of thought without the burden of having thought.

The second thing not to do with AI is use it to simulate expertise. We already live in a culture crowded with confident advice from people who have never done the work, carried the risk, or paid the cost of being wrong. AI can intensify that problem by making it easy to sound informed without being informed. A fluent answer is not the same as earned understanding, and a polished paragraph is not the same as wisdom. The danger is not that AI will make everyone sound unintelligent; the danger is that it will make too many people sound credible before they have done anything to deserve credibility.

The third thing not to do with AI is use it to dodge accountability. If a decision affects someone's job, finances, health, education, reputation, or future, then a human being has to own that decision. AI can help organize evidence, surface patterns, flag inconsistencies, or make complicated information easier to review, but it should not become the place where responsibility disappears. "The AI recommended it" is not a moral defense. It is a confession that judgment was outsourced at precisely the moment judgment was required.

The fourth thing not to do with AI is outsource empathy. There are moments when the human presence matters more than the elegance of the wording: an apology, a condolence, a difficult conversation with an employee, a message to someone who trusted you, or a response to someone who is hurt. AI may help a person find language when they are overwhelmed or afraid of saying the wrong thing, and that can be useful. But the care itself cannot be automated. If the feeling is not yours, the message becomes a performance, and people can often sense the absence even when the sentences are technically correct.

The fifth thing not to do with AI is use it to avoid learning. There is a difference between receiving help and escaping the struggle that develops competence. If AI solves every problem before you wrestle with it, you may get the answer faster, but you may also lose the growth that comes from confusion, revision, experimentation, and failure. In writing, coding, leadership, analysis, and countless other disciplines, the struggle is not merely an obstacle to the work. Very often, the struggle is the work.

For me, the boundary is straightforward. I will use AI to support my work, but I will not use it to replace my voice, my judgment, my responsibility, or my experience. I will use it to clean up the sentence, but not to invent the conviction behind it. I will use it to organize a thought, but not to pretend the thought was mine if it was not. I will use it as a tool, but I will not let it become a mask.

If AI is doing the thinking, writing, caring, deciding, and explaining, then we should be honest enough to ask what we are contributing. And if the answer is "not much," then perhaps the solution is not to publish more, automate more, or generate more content. Perhaps the solution is to live more, learn more, think more, and return to the page when we have something of our own to say.
